An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment
Technical Report

MaoXun Huang    Kshitij Kapoor    Eli Louise Affiliation: Grid Agents Email: {mao, kaps, eli}@grid-agents.com
Abstract

Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent’s tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33–67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.

1 Introduction

Grid connection, more than generation, now limits the energy transition. At least 3,000 GW of renewable projects were waiting in connection queues worldwide in 2023 [18]. In the United States alone, about 2,600 GW of generation and storage was seeking interconnection at the end of that year [45]. Both the United States and Great Britain have reformed their connection processes in response [9, 38].

Each connection request needs two kinds of expert work. Regulatory work checks the application against legislation, grid codes and standards that run to thousands of pages and change as reform proceeds. Engineering work decides where the project can connect and what reinforcement it needs, by running power-flow, contingency (N-1) and short-circuit studies on a network model [25, 63]. Both are slow and both are short of people.

Agents built on large language models (LLMs) plan, call tools and act on the results [67, 48, 61], which suits both tasks. They also fail in three ways that matter here. They write fluent text that no source supports [20]. They cannot be trusted with the arithmetic of large network equations. Finally, a correct answer does not show that the work behind it was correct. The same number can come from the right study, from memory or from a study of the wrong grid state, and most benchmarks grade only the number. Yet a connection decision commits costly network works and can be challenged by the applicant or the regulator, so the engineer must be able to show which study ran on which network.

We present Grid Agents, a system designed around these failure modes. It has two parts (Figure 2):

  • •

    The Grid Ontology is the knowledge system of Grid Agents. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable by the agents, and evolves as they learn from use, with people approving what is shared.11 1 We use ontology for an organised body of domain knowledge, not a formal specification of a conceptualisation [13]. Agents answer questions and review applications from it, and every answer rests on evidence they cite.

  • •

    Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment, with domain tools and a framework that carries a study from the choice of connection point to the final report, and it is connected to the Grid Ontology for the knowledge its studies draw on. Established solvers compute every number it reports.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    A design for agents in regulated engineering work, built on three principles, with a memory that learns from use under human approval (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    A power-system benchmark suite of 519 tasks from eight published benchmark families, on networks of 4 to 9,241 buses, graded the same way on one scale of depth (Section 4.1).

  3. 3.

    Results and findings against coding agents, retrieval pipelines, leaderboard entries and frontier models, with each agent’s work verified against the study it ran (Section 5). The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than any other system. Grid Studio leads the best coding agent in both score and agent work time, by a statistically significant margin, and its lead is largest on the biggest networks. Optimisation in the loop makes reinforcement cheaper.

2 Background and Related Work

Retrieval and citation.

Retrieval-augmented generation conditions a model on passages fetched for the question [27]. In its common form a pipeline searches once and the model answers from what comes back. The search may be lexical or dense, often followed by a reranker [47, 24, 37]. It may also run over a graph built from the corpus [7] or follow a document’s own hierarchy [58]. Longer context windows do not remove the need to retrieve well [28]. Agentic approaches instead let the model decide what to retrieve and judge what it found [1], or explore the corpus from a programming environment [69]. Because a reviewer must be able to check every source, the citations matter as much as the answer. Work on attributed generation measures whether citations support the claims [10], and model judges score faithfulness and answer quality [8, 71]. LegalBench-RAG [42], built on CUAD [15] and related to LegalBench [14], scores retrieval on exact character spans, which separates finding the right document from finding the right clause.

Tool-using agents and their evaluation.

Engineering work needs an agent that acts as well as reads. ReAct interleaves reasoning and action [67], Toolformer learns when to call a tool [48], Reflexion adds self-critique [52], AutoGen composes several agents [65] and MANTA lets a multi-agent system adapt how its agents collaborate while it runs [17]. As agents began to act, their evaluation moved from judging text to checking outcomes. SWE-bench runs a repository’s tests [22], AgentBench spans many environments [29] and τ\tau-bench compares the final database state with a goal state [68]. Our strict pass brings this state-based grading to engineering studies by checking the grid state that each study ran on.

Agent memory.

An agent that works beside the same people for months should also keep what it learns. CoALA organises a language agent’s memory into working, semantic, episodic and procedural stores [53], after the distinction drawn in human memory [57]. MemGPT pages information between the context and external storage [39]. Generative Agents and Reflexion turn experience into reflections that guide later behaviour [41, 52], ExpeL distils insights from past trajectories [70] and Voyager grows a library of skills [60]. These systems learn on their own. In regulated work, one engineer’s session must not silently change a colleague’s agent, so the memory we describe in Section 3.2 adds human approval.

Power-system studies.

In engineering work, the actions an agent takes are calls to power-system analyses whose methods are long established. A power flow solves the AC network equations for voltages and flows at one operating point [63]. Security standards require the system to survive any single credible outage [36], so a contingency (N-1) analysis repeats the power flow with each element out of service. Short-circuit, stability and dynamic studies cover fault levels and the seconds after a disturbance [25], and optimal power flow (OPF) finds the least-cost dispatch within network limits. Open-source solvers such as MATPOWER [72], pandapower [54] and PowerModels.jl [5] implement these analyses, and several benchmarks take their answer keys from them. For an engineer, and for an agent, the difficulty lies less in the computation than in choosing which studies to run on which network state, and in reading the results against the rules.

Language models for power systems.

Language models have only recently been applied to this work. Surveys map the opportunities and risks [16, 32, 11]. Agent systems include multi-agent simulation frameworks [21], agents for analysis and operations [23, 62], an agent for connection impact assessment [49] and tool servers for power-system software [43]. Several are evaluated on task sets of their own [23, 62], which makes them hard to compare. Shared benchmarks have followed. They cover power-flow questions (PFBench [50]), agentic studies (PowerAgentBench [35], PSAB [56]), natural-language study tasks (PowerCodeBench [64]), power flow under load, dispatch and topology variation (PFΔ\Delta [46], solved with Ipopt [59]) and natural-language OPF modifications (ProOPF [51]). Older datasets supply independent references, among them PGLib-OPF [2], OPFData [31], Grid2Op/L2RPN and RL2Grid [6, 34, 33] and the IEEE PES small-signal benchmark systems [4].

3 System Overview

3.1 Design principles

P1. Evidence before answers.

Every answer and finding is anchored to a passage in a source document or in the applicant’s submission.

P2. Computation by established solvers.

The model chooses, sequences and interprets studies, and solvers produce every number.

P3. Human decision authority.

Agents prepare the work and people decide. Agent verdicts sit beside human verdicts, decisions need sign-off by named people, and studies pause at decision points [40].

3.2 The Grid Ontology

Knowledge base.

The Grid Ontology holds the legislation, grid codes, standards and process documents that an application is checked against. The GB corpus in our experiments has 27 documents with 6,347 pages, including their figures and tables.

Grounded answers.

An agent answers questions and reviews applications from this knowledge base. It answers only from evidence it has found and must cite the passages its answer relies on.

Memory.

Documents state the rules, and memory holds what the agents learn while applying them. Following the CoALA taxonomy [53], it holds three kinds (Table 1).

Self-evolving memory.

All three kinds of memory change with use. Lessons drawn from recent work [41, 70] become experiences, and facts, rules and skills are added or revised as the work shows what the agents lack. A change that would affect other people takes effect only after a person approves it. The agents therefore improve with use while every shared change stays visible and attributable, which is principle P3 applied to learning.

3.3 Grid Studio

Studies through established solvers.

Grid Studio gives the agent power-system studies as tools. The agent chooses which studies to run and on which network state, and reads the results, while established solvers compute every number (P2).

Reinforcement planning.

When a project needs reinforcement, the agent calls an optimiser that proposes the least-cost package of works, in the spirit of transmission expansion planning [26]. Section 5.2 evaluates it.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Benchmarks

Table 2 lists the benchmarks and what each tests. We also give every task a depth, how much work the system must do to reach the answer, in the spirit of PowerCodeBench’s difficulty levels [64]. Figures 3 and 4 place each benchmark on this scale, and Table 6 in Appendix A gives an example of each step.

Regulatory knowledge.

The GB Regulation Set is our own set of 45 questions on GB grid regulation, asked of the 27 documents of the GB corpus (6,347 pages). An R1 question is answered by one passage, an R2 question by a figure or table, and an R3 question only by combining passages. We built it evidence first. Passages and figures are sampled from the corpus, a model writes a question from each, questions the evidence does not support or that need no evidence are discarded, and the domain owner approves the rest (Appendix D). The Enterprise RAG Challenge asks similar questions of 100 company annual reports (14,454 pages), and about half have no answer in the reports, so the system must also recognise when there is none. LegalBench-RAG (R4) asks for the exact span of a clause in a long contract, and we use a fixed sample of 50 questions from its CUAD subset [15], whose 462 contracts are plain text without pages (about 3.9 million words). ViDoRe V3 [30] asks 2,419 questions of 19,252 pages of visually rich documents in English and French, and scores the ranking of the pages a system returns. Its own question labels give each question a depth (Appendix D).

Power-system engineering.

Eight benchmark families give 519 tasks on networks of 4 to 9,241 buses. An L1 task runs one study on the network as published, an L2 task first applies stated changes, and an L3 task must first find what to change, such as the most heavily loaded line. An L4 task rebuilds a published operating point of 20 to 261 values, and an L5 task turns a written requirement into a changed optimisation problem. None poses a multi-stage study, so Section 5.2 measures one separately.

4.2 Evaluation metrics

Regulatory knowledge.

We score the evidence each system cites. A cited item matches a gold anchor if it comes from the same document and overlaps the anchor’s span, lies within one page of it, or is the anchored figure. We report recall, precision, MRR, nDCG@10 [19] and hit rate, and a model judge marks each answer against the gold answer [71]. LegalBench-RAG and the Enterprise RAG Challenge keep their own metrics and scoring script, and ViDoRe V3 its board’s nDCG@10, averaged over its sets.

Power-system engineering.

A correct number can come from memory, a lucky guess or a study on the wrong grid state, so we grade the work behind each answer as well as the answer. A task is a strict pass only if its answer is within the benchmark’s tolerance and the system’s recorded work shows that the required study ran on the required grid state. With numeric closeness c¯\bar{c}, answer accuracy AA and strict pass rate PP, each taken over all nn tasks, the end-to-end score is

E= 0.25​c¯+ 0.25​A+ 0.5​P.E\;=\;0.25\,\bar{c}\;+\;0.25\,A\;+\;0.5\,P. (1)

A base model, which answers without tools, gets the network as text in its prompt and reports the solved states its answer rests on, which we check against our own solution. Appendix B defines each term, describes how the work of each kind of system is verified, and gives the reasons for the weights.

4.3 Evaluation method

Systems compared.

On the regulatory benchmarks we compare the Grid Ontology with a general coding agent (Claude Code) that has the corpus as files and its own file and shell tools, with one-shot retrieval pipelines that search once and answer from their top eight results, and on the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3 with their published entries. On the power-system benchmarks we compare Grid Studio with two coding agents as shipped, Claude Code and Codex CLI on GPT-6.1 sol, each with a shell, Python and the network as a file. We also compare it with Power-Agent [43, 44], which installs PowerMCP’s pandapower tools and PowerSkills’ playbooks into Claude Code, and with eleven base models, which answer without tools from the network given as text, among them the frontier models GPT-6.1 sol and Fable 5.1. Claude Code and Power-Agent run on the same model as our agents, and Power-Agent uses its tools and playbooks as their authors publish them. We also time each system’s agent work, the time it spends on model turns and tool runs. Appendix D gives the evaluation protocol.

5 Results

5.1 Grid Ontology

Table 3 gives the results on all four benchmarks. On the GB Regulation Set and LegalBench-RAG, every system answers with the same model, so the differences come from the evidence each finds and cites. On the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3, the Grid Ontology is first on the public board.

GB Regulation Set.

Both agents answer every question correctly, so the evidence they cite is what separates them. The Grid Ontology cites the right evidence for more questions than Claude Code (recall 0.967 against 0.856), and the gap is widest on single-passage questions that ask for a number (1.000 against 0.625). This matters in review, where a correct answer that cites the wrong passage still has to be checked by hand. The retrieval pipelines answer fewer questions correctly. Vector retrieval with a reranker comes closest, while PageIndex and GraphRAG find the evidence for fewer than half of the questions. Example A in Appendix A shows one question.

LegalBench-RAG.

The Grid Ontology reaches an F1 of 0.980, ahead of every baseline. It cites one contract per question, while the retrieval pipelines cite up to five, so the right contract is usually among theirs but so are wrong ones. Its one miss is a contract filed twice, where it cited the signed copy and the answer key names the unsigned draft. At the benchmark’s stricter clause level, its lead over the pipelines is an order of magnitude (Appendix E).

Enterprise RAG Challenge.

The challenge’s own script scores both the exact answers and the pages they cite, out of 150 [55]. The Grid Ontology scores 124.5 against 123.7 for the best published entry, and it correctly declines 45 of the 51 questions that the reports cannot answer.

ViDoRe V3.

The board scores the first ten pages returned for each English question by nDCG@10, averaged over eight public sets. The Grid Ontology scores 70.23 against 70.01 for the best published pipeline and leads on four of the eight sets (Appendix F).

5.2 Grid Studio

Table 4 gives the mean end-to-end score over the eight benchmark families, and Table 8 gives each family. Grid Studio scores 99.9%, with 100% on seven of the eight families and 99.2% on PowerCodeBench, statistically significantly above every other system. Codex CLI scores 99.4%, but 19 of its 23 misses are on networks above 2,000 buses, and it takes up to 55% longer per task. Power-Agent also scores 99.4%, and Grid Studio scores higher on 13 tasks and lower on one, with Grid Studio’s time 0.75 of Power-Agent’s on the same task. Claude Code scores 85.4%.

Base models.

The best base model, GPT-6.1 sol, answers 250 of the 519 tasks (48%) correctly. Given the network as text, the strongest base models solve small power flows by hand, but none has its work verified on a network of more than 39 buses. None answers more than 30% of the PFΔ\Delta tasks, where a published operating point must be solved, or more than two of the seven RL2Grid tasks, where switching actions must be compared, and none scores above 41% end to end.

Score against time.

Figure 1 sets each score against the agent work time. Grid Studio needs a median of 13.9 s per task, against at most 21.6 s for Codex CLI and 22.0 s for Claude Code, so it scores highest in the least time. Reading the network and writing out the solved states takes the base models a median of 20 s to almost 3 minutes per task, so every other system is both slower than Grid Studio and lower scoring. More time does not close the gap: GPT-6.1 sol and Fable 5.1 spend about 1 and 3 minutes per task and still stay below 41%.

Domain tools must reach the study.

Power-Agent installs PowerMCP’s pandapower tools and PowerSkills’ playbooks into Claude Code, on the same model as Grid Studio, and comes close to Grid Studio’s score. Its PowerMCP tools were called on only 46 of the 519 tasks and settled 16 on their own. The other 503 needed the agent’s own pandapower code, and 473 never called PowerMCP at all, while a PowerSkills playbook was followed in 409. Its results therefore come mostly from code the agent writes for each task rather than from the domain tools. Grid Studio’s tools reach every study the benchmarks ask for, which is what makes its work both verifiable and fast.

Real studies are larger.

The benchmark networks have at most 9,241 buses. An operator’s planning model can run to tens of thousands of buses, and a connection study chains many studies, from screening the options to designing reinforcement. The baselines already fall short at the top of the benchmarks. Of the 109 tasks on networks above 2,000 buses, Power-Agent passes 106, Codex CLI 90 and Claude Code 74, against 108 for Grid Studio, and the base models pass none. Grid Studio takes its numbers from established solvers rather than from code written for each task, and its work can be checked at every step, which makes it the better design for real planning studies.

Optimisation makes reinforcement cheaper.

The benchmarks pose single studies, so we tested the reinforcement stage of a connection study separately. In five studies on networks of 30, 118 and 2,000 buses, the last the synthetic Texas grid ACTIVSg2000 [3], the agent designed the package twice on its own and twice with the optimiser, using the same model and catalogue of priced reinforcement works (Table 5). Both approaches cleared every overload the projects caused, as an independent AC N-1 check of each final network confirms. The optimiser’s packages were 33–67% cheaper on average.

6 Conclusion

Grid Agents is built on three principles. Answers rest on cited evidence, numbers come from established solvers, and engineers make the decisions. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG, and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. On 519 tasks from eight published power-system benchmark families, Grid Studio scores highest and needs the least agent work time, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33–67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.

Appendix

 

Appendix A Example Questions and Tasks

Table 6 gives one question per depth level. Examples A and A are regulatory questions, and Examples A to A are power-system tasks with their strict-pass checks.

Appendix B Power-System Metrics

Each power-system task is graded on the answer a system reports and on the work that produced it. This appendix defines the terms of Eq. 1, how the work is verified and why the terms are weighted as they are.

Why the work is graded.

Most answers are voltages, loadings or costs on standard IEEE and PGLib networks, so a value can be recalled from published results, guessed close to the truth or reached by a study on the wrong grid state. An engineer acts on a result only when the study behind it is known to be right, so only a correct answer with verified work earns full credit.

Terms for one task.

For task ii, let aia_{i} be the reported value and gig_{i} the answer key, compared at the benchmark’s own tolerance.

  • •

    Correct answer: ri=1r_{i}=1 if aia_{i} is within tolerance of gig_{i} and every named choice, such as the outage pair in Example A, matches the key, and ri=0r_{i}=0 otherwise.

  • •

    Verified work: vi=1v_{i}=1 if the recorded work shows the required study on the required grid state, and vi=0v_{i}=0 otherwise.

  • •

    Strict pass: si=ri​vis_{i}=r_{i}\,v_{i}.

  • •

    Numeric closeness: ci=1c_{i}=1 within tolerance, and max⁡(0, 1−|ai−gi|/max⁡(|gi|,1))\max\bigl(0,\,1-|a_{i}-g_{i}|/\max(|g_{i}|,1)\bigr) otherwise.

AA, PP and c¯\bar{c} are the means of rir_{i}, sis_{i} and cic_{i} over all nn tasks, so EE is the mean of ei=0.25​ci+0.25​ri+0.5​sie_{i}=0.25\,c_{i}+0.25\,r_{i}+0.5\,s_{i}. A task scores 1 when its answer is correct and its work verified, 0.5 when only its answer is correct, at most 0.25 when its answer is wrong and 0 when it has no answer. Tasks a system cannot execute, for example for lack of a tool, stay in the mean. Leaving them out would grade that system on an easier subset.

Verifying the work.

The required work comes from the task, never from the answer key: the grid state the question fixes (the published network with every stated change), the type of study, any stated study arguments and, for a comparison, every candidate state. Table 7 shows what is checked for each kind of system. A value the base case already holds may be restated or left as it is, but any other change, such as an extra open line, makes a different state and fails.

The coding agents and the base models solve the network in their own code or by themselves, so they report with their answer the solved states it rests on. We solve the required network ourselves and accept a power flow when the reported voltages match ours at every bus within 10−410^{-4} pu and 0.01∘0.01^{\circ}, up to a common angle shift, an N-1 or a comparison when each of its states does, and an OPF when its dispatch balances and respects every limit of the required network. In a control on 31 sampled tasks, this check accepted every correct state and rejected states solved with a required change left out, apart from two OPF tasks where that change does not bind. Base models receive the network as text in their prompt, or the question alone where the network is too large to fit.

Why these weights.

Strict pass carries half the weight because it is the result that matters in use, so a system whose work cannot be shown reaches at most half the score. Answer accuracy carries a quarter, so a correct answer without verified work still beats a wrong one. Closeness carries the last quarter. It equals 1 on every correct answer and only separates a near miss from a large error. A guess at a per-unit voltage near 1 earns much of it, so it never decides a pass.

Appendix C Full Results on the Power-System Benchmarks

Table 8 gives the end-to-end score of every system on the 519 tasks, and Figure 5 shows how much each system’s results vary across families and tasks.

Appendix D Evaluation Protocol Details

GB Regulation Set.

Pages and figures are sampled from the corpus with a seeded generator, never through the system under test. A model sees only the sampled passage or figure and writes a question, its answer and verbatim quotations. Separate checks discard questions the evidence does not support and questions answerable without it [12], and the domain owner approves the rest. Each question keeps its evidence anchors (document, page, character span or figure). The 45 questions (25 text, 14 figure, 6 multi-hop) come from 23 of the 27 documents.

ViDoRe V3 depth.

From the benchmark’s own labels, the 203 multi-hop questions are R3, the 1,312 others answered from a table, chart, infographic or image are R2, and the remaining 904 are R1.

Power-system questions.

Every task is posed as a question about a stated network with one value to report, so that every system receives the same wording and is graded the same way. PFBench, PowerCodeBench and ProOPF-B publish such questions, and we ask them in their authors’ words. Where one omits a quantity or choice its answer depends on (156 of 352 PowerCodeBench and 6 of 19 ProOPF-B items), we restore it from the item’s own record, never adding the answer. PFΔ\Delta and PGLib-OPF publish networks and solved results but no questions, so we pose each task from a fixed template that names the network, any stated changes and the quantity to report. PowerAgentBench-SS releases task specifications without a question set, PSAB’s tasks are built for agents that work on files, and RL2Grid scores reinforcement-learning episodes rather than answers. For these three we keep the kind of study each one tests and write the questions ourselves, with answers from a reference solver. In all, 389 of the 519 questions are in their authors’ words and 130 are ours. Ours come from fixed templates, not from a language model.

Answer keys.

Answer keys never come from the system under test. The regulatory keys are the published ones, apart from the GB Regulation Set’s, which the domain owner approved. PFBench, PowerCodeBench and ProOPF-B use their authors’ published answers, PFΔ\Delta its authors’ Ipopt solutions, and PGLib-OPF its published OPF baseline, with a reference solver for its power-flow tasks. The three adapted families (Table 2) are graded against a reference solver, so we treat them as weaker evidence. Run with no model, the reference solver reproduces every published answer of PFBench, PFΔ\Delta, PowerCodeBench and ProOPF-B (460 tasks), so a solver discrepancy is never counted as an agent failure.

Isolation.

Each coding-agent task runs in its own container (2 vCPU, 8 GB) with no answer key and no network access, and a task that fetched anything would count as unanswered. None did. An audit of every GB Regulation Set run with file access found no read of an answer key. Grid Studio runs with memory off, and its timed runs use the same container size, one task per container.

Agent work time.

Agent work is the time spent on model turns and tool runs, read from each agent’s own clock. It excludes start-up, which covers launching and tearing down the container and starting the agent and, for Grid Studio, its solvers. Codex CLI reports no such split, so its time is the whole run of its process, an upper bound. A base model spends all its time on one completion. Figure 1 reports the median over the 519 tasks. A coding agent loads its libraries inside its own scripts, while starting Grid Studio’s solvers, 6.7 s on average when we measured it, is not counted.

Systems compared.

Table 9 gives each system’s version and setting. The two base models in the table and the nine further ones in Figure 1 and Table 8 ran on the same 519 tasks between 29 and 31 October 2026, each with the network in its prompt, and were graded with the same grader. Grid Studio, Power-Agent and the base models ran once per task, and Codex CLI and Claude Code once on PowerCodeBench and five times on the other families. Power-Agent ran on 2 November 2026 in the same sandbox as the coding agents, with no network access beyond the model. GPT-5.6 sol lost 26 PowerCodeBench tasks and GPT-6.1 sol 3 to provider quota limits, counted as unanswered, and Fable 5.1 answered 146 PowerCodeBench questions in their earlier wording. Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5 reached the reply limit without an answer on 170 and 128 tasks, and Fable 5.1 refused 115. Where a provider’s quota ran out during a run, the remaining tasks ran on the same model through another provider (GPT-6.1 sol and Sonnet 5.5). Grid Studio’s tools were extended where a benchmark, PowerCodeBench among them, asked for a study they did not yet cover, and the affected benchmarks were run again.

Appendix E LegalBench-RAG Details

Table 3 scores LegalBench-RAG by document. Precision is the share of cited contracts that hold the answer, and recall the share of answer-holding contracts that were cited. The benchmark’s own metrics are stricter and score the character overlap between the cited text and the gold clause. Table 10 gives both.

At the clause level, agentic systems reach an F1 an order of magnitude above retrieval pipelines (0.47 to 0.62 against 0.03 to 0.09), so pipelines find the right contract but not the clause. In a sweep over chunking, hybrid search and embeddings [66], no pipeline configuration exceeded a clause F1 of 0.13. PageIndex reaches clause recall 0.72 but precision 0.05, because it returns whole sections. The Grid Ontology leads on both clause and document F1, and Example A shows what clause-level scoring rewards.

Appendix F ViDoRe V3 Details

Table 11 gives the ViDoRe V3 scores of Table 3 per set. The Grid Ontology leads on four of the eight sets, VisAgentRet on three and EVIE-4.5B with JEV-27B-VL on physics. We chose the agent’s settings on the first 40 questions of each set, then ran all 2,419 questions. One question ended in an error and is left out of its set’s mean (counted as zero, the mean is 70.20).
